title: Second US Judge Blocks Trump's $100,000 H-1B Fee in Oakland Ruling
excerpt: Judge Haywood Gilliam ruled USCIS and the State Department skipped required rulemaking before imposing the fee, granting unions and employers a block while their lawsuit proceeds — the second such defeat after Boston's June ruling.
body:
• In the second major court defeat for the fee, US District Judge Haywood Gilliam in Oakland, California, ruled September 30 that USCIS and the State Department failed to follow required rulemaking processes before implementing the $100,000 charge on new H-1B visas.
  • Gilliam, an Obama appointee, granted a coalition of unions, employers, and nonprofits an order blocking the agencies from implementing the fee while their October lawsuit proceeds — the same day it was the fee's original expiration, after Trump extended it another year.
  • The ruling follows a June decision by a Boston federal judge (in a 20-state lawsuit) temporarily blocking the fee, which a Boston appeals court refused to pause in July.
  • Separately, the Department of Homeland Security moved in August to adopt a permanent ~$103,000 fee — a different legal battle that will face fresh court challenges — and the US Chamber of Commerce has filed a third lawsuit now under appeal.

A second federal judge has blocked the $100,000 fee that US President Donald Trump imposed on new H-1B visas for highly skilled foreign workers. US District Judge Haywood Gilliam in Oakland, California, ruled on September 30 that US Citizenship and Immigration Services and the State Department failed to follow necessary rule-making processes before implementing the fee, granting a coalition of unions, employers, and nonprofits an order blocking its enforcement while their lawsuit proceeds.

The ruling is a fresh blow to the administration's signature immigration charge. The fee was originally set to expire September 21, but Trump recently extended it for another year — making the timing of Gilliam's order particularly significant. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Context & Background

This is not the fee's first courtroom loss. In June, a federal judge in Boston temporarily blocked the charge in a separate case brought by 20 states, and a Boston-based appeals court in July declined to pause that decision. Gilliam, appointed by then-President Barack Obama, is now the second judge to find the agencies' implementation unlawful.

The legal argument at the heart of both cases is about presidential power and procedure, not immigration policy itself. Trump created the fee through a September 2025 presidential proclamation covering many new H-1B workers hired from outside the United States, and federal agencies issued guidance explaining which petitions would require the payment and how employers could pay it. Gilliam found the agencies should have gone through the notice-and-comment process required by the Administrative Procedure Act — publishing proposed rules, taking public comment, and considering those comments — before implementing the policies.

His order applies both to agency policies implementing the original proclamation and to Trump's September extension of the $100,000 requirement. The plaintiffs include Global Nurse Force, a California-based company that recruits nurses for US health care facilities. Democracy Forward, the left-leaning legal group representing the plaintiffs, applauded the ruling: "Today's decision ... protects a system that was thrown into chaos overnight," said Steve Bressler, a lawyer with the group.

Impact & Analysis

For employers — and for the Indian professionals who dominate H-1B hiring — the ruling means the fee cannot be collected while the October lawsuit moves forward. The H-1B program is the primary legal pathway for skilled Indian workers into the US tech industry, and a $100,000 per-worker surcharge would have fundamentally altered the economics of hiring Indian talent, hitting outsourcing firms and US employers alike.

But the fight is far from over. In August, DHS moved to adopt a permanent fee of about $103,000 — a separate rulemaking that will face its own court challenges. The administration could appeal Gilliam's order, and the US Chamber of Commerce has filed a third lawsuit and is appealing a judge's rejection of its claims that Trump had no authority to set the fee.

The pattern emerging is a multi-front legal war: two judges have now blocked the original proclamation-based fee, while the administration pursues a permanent fee through formal rulemaking — a harder target, but one that has already drawn coordinated legal opposition from business groups, unions, and states.

Diaspora Angle

Indian nationals are by far the largest group of H-1B recipients, and Indian IT services firms are among the biggest sponsors. Every twist in the fee battle directly affects thousands of Indian families' employment plans — and the uncertainty alone has already reshaped hiring behavior, with some employers delaying or restructuring petitions. A second judicial block restores the status quo for now, but the administration's push for a permanent $103,000 fee means the reprieve may be temporary.

What's Next

The October lawsuit will now proceed with the fee blocked in the meantime. Watch for the administration's appeal of Gilliam's order, the progress of DHS's permanent-fee rulemaking, and the Chamber of Commerce's appeal in its third case. The fee's original September 21 expiry has passed, but Trump's extension keeps the legal stakes — and the uncertainty for employers — fully alive.
